passage_title: Light and Photosynthesis in Sun and Shade Leaves
passage:
In photosynthesis, a leaf takes up carbon dioxide (CO2) and uses light energy to make sugar. At the same time, the leaf releases CO2 through respiration. A leaf's net photosynthesis rate is the rate at which it takes up CO2 minus the rate at which it releases CO2; a negative net rate means the leaf is releasing more CO2 than it is taking up. Leaves that grow in full sun and leaves that grow in shade can respond differently to light, even on the same tree.

Researchers selected 10 leaves that had grown in full sun at the top of a maple tree's crown and 10 leaves that had grown in deep shade near the bottom of the same crown. Each leaf, still attached to the tree, was sealed in a clear chamber kept at 25 °C, and a lamp exposed it to light at eight different intensities, measured in micromoles of photons per square meter per second (µmol photons/m²/s). At each intensity, the leaf's net photosynthesis rate was measured in micromoles of CO2 per square meter of leaf per second (µmol CO2/m²/s). Table 1 shows the average net photosynthesis rates.

graphic.caption: Table 1. Average net photosynthesis rate of sun leaves and shade leaves at eight light intensities

prompt: According to Table 1, at a light intensity of 400 µmol photons/m²/s, the average net photosynthesis rate of the shade leaves was:
choices: 4.4 µmol CO2/m²/s
5.0 µmol CO2/m²/s
8.6 µmol CO2/m²/s
11.2 µmol CO2/m²/s
correct_answer: 5.0 µmol CO2/m²/s
explanation: In the 400 µmol photons/m²/s row, the shade leaves column reads 5.0. The value 4.4 is the shade leaves at 200 µmol photons/m²/s, 8.6 is the sun leaves at 400, and 11.2 is the sun leaves at 800.

Duckweed is a tiny plant that floats on the surface of ponds. Each plant consists of one or more flat, leaflike fronds, and the population grows as existing fronds bud off new fronds. Experiment 1

They counted the fronds in each container on Days 0, 4, 8, and 12.

Experiment 2
Students repeated the procedure of Experiment 1 with 3 new containers, each with a phosphate concentration of 2.0 mg/L. The containers were kept at 15 °C, 25 °C, and 35 °C, respectively.

Table 1 shows the results of both experiments.

passage:
In a tropical forest, adult trees of a species called Species T produce large fruits, each containing one seed. Monkeys and bats eat some of the fruits and drop the seeds as far as 100 m away, but most fruits fall beneath the parent tree's crown, which extends about 10 m from the trunk. Researchers marked 1,000 newly sprouted Species T seedlings within 5 m of adult Species T trees and 1,000 newly sprouted seedlings 30 m from the nearest adult Species T tree. After 1 year, 3% of the seedlings near adults and 27% of the seedlings 30 m away were still alive. Two scientists explain why seedlings near adults survive so poorly.

Scientist 1
Seedlings near adults die mainly because of natural enemies that specialize on Species T. A species of beetle and a soil fungus attack only Species T. Because each adult drops fruit beneath its crown year after year, these enemies build up in large numbers in the soil and leaf litter there. A Species T seedling near an adult is therefore almost certain to be attacked, while one 30 m away is usually not found by the enemies. Seedlings of other tree species growing beneath Species T adults are not harmed by these enemies. Even after an adult dies, the fungus survives for several years in its dead roots, so seedlings near the spot remain at risk.

Scientist 2
Seedlings near adults die mainly because the adults take the resources the seedlings need. An adult's dense crown blocks most of the sunlight, and its roots, which are densest within about 10 m of the trunk, take up most of the water and nutrients in the soil there. Seedlings of any species growing beneath a Species T adult are short of light, water, and nutrients and grow too slowly to survive. Seedlings 30 m away are beyond the adult's crown and its densest roots, so they receive more of these resources. Insects and fungi do attack seedlings, but they kill mainly seedlings of any species that are already weakened by a lack of resources; well-supplied seedlings survive attack.

passage_title: The Cause of a Side Stitch
passage:
A side stitch is a sharp pain felt at one spot on one side of the abdomen, usually just below the ribs, during exercise. It is reported by about 70% of regular runners each year and is also common among horseback riders. Stitches are more frequent when a person has eaten a meal or drunk a large volume of liquid within 2 hours before exercising, and some stitches are accompanied by pain at the tip of the shoulder. The diaphragm is the dome-shaped sheet of muscle beneath the lungs that contracts when a person inhales. The parietal peritoneum is a thin membrane that lines the inside of the abdominal wall. Pain at the tip of the shoulder can result from irritation of tissues served by the phrenic nerve. Two scientists discuss the cause of side stitches.

Scientist 1
A stitch is a cramp of the diaphragm caused by reduced blood flow to it. The liver, stomach, and spleen hang from the underside of the diaphragm by ligaments. During running or riding, each time the body lands, these organs are jolted downward and tug on the diaphragm while it is also working hard to move air. The repeated tugging squeezes the diaphragm's blood vessels and reduces its blood supply, and the muscle cramps. A full stomach adds weight and increases the tug. Because the diaphragm is served by the phrenic nerve, pain from the diaphragm can be felt at the shoulder tip. Stitches should therefore occur mainly in activities that involve repeated up-and-down jolting of the torso.

Scientist 2
A stitch is caused by irritation of the parietal peritoneum. This lining is rich in pain-sensing nerve endings that can pinpoint the location of an irritation, which is why a stitch is felt at one sharp spot. When the stomach is swollen with food or drink, it presses against the lining and rubs against it as the torso moves. Bending the spine forward also presses the abdominal organs against the lining, so a stitch is more likely when a person exercises in a hunched posture. The part of the parietal peritoneum just beneath the diaphragm is also served by the phrenic nerve, so irritation there can produce shoulder-tip pain. Jolting is not required; any activity that repeatedly moves the torso against a full stomach, including twisting, can produce a stitch.

choices: irritation of the abdominal lining.
a cramp in the abdominal wall.
a cramp in the diaphragm.
the liver pressing on the ribs.
correct_answer: a cramp in the diaphragm.
explanation: Scientist 1 states that "a stitch is a cramp of the diaphragm caused by reduced blood flow to it." Irritation of the abdominal lining is Scientist 2's explanation, and Scientist 1 says nothing about cramps of the abdominal wall or about the liver pressing on the ribs; the liver tugs on the diaphragm.
